summary.text: At \(n=140\), rational bounds on \(\sqrt{5/4}\) give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). The claimed relation would instead require \(a(161)=528+484-471=541\), so this instance is a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor,
\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating it at the single valid index \(n=140\).

Put
\[
x=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
We will need the values of \(\lfloor kx\rfloor\) for
\(k=140,144,157,161\). Recall that, for an integer \(m\),
\(\lfloor y\rfloor=m\) exactly when
\[
m\le y<m+1.
\]
All rational numbers compared with \(x\) below are positive. Since
\(x^2=5/4\), their comparisons with \(x\) can therefore be established
by squaring: for positive \(q\), the inequality \(q\le x\) follows from
\(q^2\le 5/4\), and \(x<q\) follows from \(5/4<q^2\).

First consider \(140x\). For the lower bound, dividing by \(140>0\), it
is enough to show
\[
\frac{156}{140}=\frac{39}{35}\le x.
\]
After squaring, this is
\[
\frac{1521}{1225}\le\frac54,
\]
which follows on cross-multiplication from
\[
4\cdot 1521=6084\le6125=5\cdot1225.
\]
For the upper bound, it is enough to show
\[
x<\frac{157}{140}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
\frac54<\frac{157^2}{140^2}=\frac{24649}{19600},
\]
and this holds because
\[
5\cdot19600=98000<98596=4\cdot24649.
\]
Equivalently, after cancelling a factor of \(4\), this is the integer
comparison \(24500<24649\). Thus
\[
156\le140x<157,
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lfloor140x\right\rfloor=156.
\]

Next consider \(144x\). The lower bound is obtained from
\[
\frac{160}{144}=\frac{10}{9}\le x,
\]
since, after squaring,
\[
\frac{100}{81}\le\frac54
\]
is equivalent to
\[
400\le405.
\]
For the upper bound,
\[
x<\frac{161}{144}
\]
follows by squaring, because
\[
\frac54<\frac{161^2}{144^2}=\frac{25921}{20736}
\]
is equivalent to
\[
5\cdot20736=103680<103684=4\cdot25921.
\]
Consequently,
\[
160\le144x<161,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor144x\right\rfloor=160.
\]

For \(157x\), first
\[
\frac{175}{157}\le x.
\]
Indeed, squaring this proposed inequality reduces it to
\[
\frac{175^2}{157^2}=\frac{30625}{24649}\le\frac54,
\]
which is true because
\[
4\cdot30625=122500\le123245=5\cdot24649.
\]
Likewise,
\[
x<\frac{176}{157},
\]
because after squaring this becomes
\[
\frac54<\frac{176^2}{157^2}=\frac{30976}{24649},
\]
and cross-multiplication gives the true inequality
\[
5\cdot24649=123245<123904=4\cdot30976.
\]
It follows that
\[
175\le157x<176,
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor157x\right\rfloor=175.
\]

Finally, for \(161x\), the lower bound
\[
\frac{180}{161}\le x
\]
follows after squaring from
\[
\frac{180^2}{161^2}=\frac{32400}{25921}\le\frac54,
\]
since
\[
4\cdot32400=129600\le129605=5\cdot25921.
\]
The upper bound
\[
x<\frac{181}{161}
\]
follows after squaring from
\[
\frac54<\frac{181^2}{161^2}=\frac{32761}{25921},
\]
since
\[
5\cdot25921=129605<131044=4\cdot32761.
\]
Thus
\[
180\le161x<181,
\]
which proves
\[
\left\lfloor161x\right\rfloor=180.
\]

We can now evaluate the four terms appearing in the recurrence at
\(n=140\). The ordinary quarter floors are
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{140}{4}\right\rfloor=35,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{144}{4}\right\rfloor=36,
\]
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{157}{4}\right\rfloor=39,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{161}{4}\right\rfloor=40.
\]
(The latter two follow respectively from \(156\le157<160\) and
\(160\le161<164\).) Combining these with the radical-floor values gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(140)
 &=2\cdot140+156+35
 =280+156+35
 =471,\\
a(144)
 &=2\cdot144+160+36
 =288+160+36
 =484,\\
a(157)
 &=2\cdot157+175+39
 =314+175+39
 =528,\\
a(161)
 &=2\cdot161+180+40
 =322+180+40
 =542.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the conjectured recurrence held for every \(n\ge1\), then at
\(n=140\) it would say
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140),
\]
because \(140+21=161\), \(140+17=157\), and \(140+4=144\). But the
right-hand side is
\[
528+484-471=1012-471=541,
\]
whereas the left-hand side is
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the asserted equality would require \(542=541\), which is false.
Since \(140\ge1\), this is a counterexample in the stated range, and the
conjecture is disproved.
